docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register Notes Hi! Casual The most common everyday greeting. Hello! Neutral Appropriate almost everywhere. Hey! Casual Friendly and informal. Good morning! Neutral Morning greeting. Good afternoon! Neutral Afternoon greeting. Good evening! Neutral Evening greeting.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
• "Hi!" is the safest everyday greeting.
  • "Hello!" is slightly more neutral.
  • "Hey!" is informal.
  • Time-based greetings are common in workplaces and customer-facing situations.

docs.text:

docs.title: ❌ Mistake
docs.text: Hello, myself Rahul.

docs.title: ✅ Natural English
docs.text: Hi! I'm Rahul.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: Native speakers introduce themselves with "I'm...", not "Myself...".

docs.title: Similar English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Difference Hi there! Slightly warmer. Hey there! More informal. Morning! Casual version of "Good morning."

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: When in doubt, say Hi!

docs.title: Hindi → English
docs.text: अरे, हाय! बहुत दिनों बाद मिले।

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
Most common: Hi!

Avoid: Hello, myself Rahul.

Remember: English greetings usually continue with small talk.

docs.text: Expression Register Notes What brings you here? Neutral Best all-purpose choice. How come you're here? Casual Friendly surprise. What are you doing here? Casual Tone matters. Fancy seeing you here! Casual Expresses pleasant surprise. Didn't expect to see you here! Casual Natural reaction.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: These expressions express surprise at unexpectedly meeting someone. They usually start a friendly conversation.

docs.title: Memory Tip

Hindi: फिर मिलेंगे!

Natural English: See you around!

docs.title: 📱 Phone
docs.text:
Hindi: ठीक है, फिर बात करेंगे।

Natural English: Talk to you soon.

docs.title: 🎓 Conference
docs.text:
Hindi: संपर्क में रहेंगे।

Natural English: Let's stay in touch.

docs.title: 🏠 Neighbour
docs.text:

Natural English: Hope to see you again soon.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake
docs.text: We will meet again and again.

docs.title: ✅ Natural English
docs.text: Keep in touch.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: Native speakers usually express staying connected rather than repeatedly meeting.

docs.title: Similar English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Difference Catch you later. Informal. Speak soon. Phone/chat. Until next time. Warm farewell.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Think stay connected, not keep meeting.

docs.title: Hindi → English
docs.text: संपर्क में रहना।

docs.title: English → Hindi
docs.text: Let's stay in touch.

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
Most common: Keep in touch.

Phone: Talk to you soon.

Avoid: We will meet again and again.

docs.title: Pattern Family 11 — Starting a Conversation Naturally
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• और बताओ।
  • और सुनाओ।
  • क्या चल रहा है?
  • क्या नया?
  • और क्या हाल?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register Notes What's been going on? Casual Great after not talking for a while. What's new? Casual Asks for recent updates. How have things been? Neutral Friendly and natural. What's been keeping you busy? Neutral Focuses on recent activities. So, what's going on? Casual Good conversation opener.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: These expressions invite conversation rather than asking for a detailed report.

docs.title: 👥 Friends
docs.text:
Hindi: और बताओ, क्या चल रहा है?

Natural English: So, what's been going on?

docs.title: 💼 Office
docs.text:
Hindi: और, प्रोजेक्ट कैसा चल रहा है?

Natural English: So, how have things been with the project?

docs.title: ☕ Café
docs.text:
Hindi: क्या नया?

Natural English: What's new?

docs.title: 📱 Phone
docs.text:
Hindi: और सुनाओ, सब ठीक?

Natural English: What's been going on? Everything good?

docs.title: 🏠 Family
docs.text:
Hindi: और क्या हाल?

Natural English: How have things been?

docs.title: ❌ Mistake
docs.text: Tell me more.

docs.title: ✅ Natural English
docs.text: What's been going on?

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: "Tell me more" is used after someone has already started speaking, not as a greeting.

docs.title: Similar English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Difference How's everything? General well-being. Anything new? Recent updates. How's life? Broader and informal.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Think of these as conversation openers.

docs.title: Hindi → English
docs.text: और बताओ, आजकल क्या चल रहा है?

docs.title: English → Hindi
docs.text: What's new?

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
Most common: What's new?

Best opener: What's been going on?

Avoid: Tell me more.

docs.title: Pattern Family 12 — Asking About Someone's Availability
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• फ्री हो?
  • बिज़ी तो नहीं हो?
  • दो मिनट हैं?
  • टाइम है?
  • अभी बात कर सकते हो?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register Do you have a minute? Neutral Got a minute? Casual Are you busy right now? Neutral Is now a good time? Neutral Can we talk for a minute? Neutral

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: These expressions politely check whether someone is available before starting a conversation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Do you have a minute?
  • Got a minute?
  • Is now a good time to talk?
  • Are you busy right now?
  • Can we talk for a minute?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Are you free?

✅ Do you have a minute?

Why? Native speakers often ask about time rather than "freedom."

docs.title: Similar English Expressions
docs.text:
• Do you have a few minutes?
  • Mind if I ask you something?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Ask for a minute, not whether someone is free.

docs.title: Mini Practice
docs.text:
Hindi → English: बिज़ी तो नहीं हो?

English → Hindi: Is now a good time?

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text: Most common: Do you have a minute?

docs.title: Pattern Family 13 — Excusing Yourself Before Speaking
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• एक बात पूछनी थी।
  • एक बात कहनी थी।
  • अगर बुरा न मानो...
  • परेशान तो नहीं कर रहा?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Can I ask you something?
  • I wanted to ask you something.
  • Do you have a quick second?
  • I hope I'm not bothering you.
  • Can I run something by you?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Used to soften the start of a conversation or request.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Can I ask you something?
  • I hope I'm not bothering you.
  • Do you have a quick second?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ One thing I wanted to tell.

✅ I wanted to tell you something.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Soften the opening before making your request.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• सुनो...
  • ज़रा सुनना...
  • अरे सुनो...
  • एक मिनट...

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Excuse me.
  • Hey.
  • Listen.
  • Can I get your attention for a second?
  • One second.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Choose expressions based on familiarity and formality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Excuse me, could you help me?
  • Hey, listen.
  • One second, please.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Listen me.

✅ Listen.

✅ Listen to me.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: It's "listen to someone", not "listen someone".

docs.title: Pattern Family 15 — Checking If Someone Can Hear You
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• मेरी आवाज़ आ रही है?
  • सुन पा रहे हो?
  • हेलो, सुन रहे हो?
  • आवाज़ कट रही है?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Can you hear me?
  • Can you hear me clearly?
  • Are you able to hear me?
  • Is my voice breaking up?
  • Can you hear me okay?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Used mainly during phone or video calls to confirm audio quality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Can you hear me?
  • Can you hear me clearly?
  • Is my voice breaking up?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Is my voice coming?

✅ Can you hear me?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Ask what the listener can hear, not what your voice is doing.

docs.title: Pattern Family 16 — Ending a Conversation Politely
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• अच्छा, चलता हूँ।
  • ठीक है, फिर बात करते हैं।
  • अब निकलता हूँ।
  • चलता हूँ फिर।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• I'd better get going.
  • I'll let you go.
  • Talk to you later.
  • See you later.
  • I've got to run.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Native speakers often soften departures instead of saying "I'm leaving."

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• I'd better get going.
  • I'll let you get back to work.
  • Talk to you later.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ I am going.

✅ I'd better get going.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: End naturally instead of announcing you're leaving.

docs.title: Pattern Family 17 — Asking Someone to Wait
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• एक मिनट।
  • ज़रा रुको।
  • थोड़ी देर रुको।
  • बस दो मिनट।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Just a second.
  • Hang on.
  • Hold on.
  • Give me a minute.
  • One moment, please.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Choose expressions based on formality. "Hang on" is casual; "One moment, please" is more formal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Hang on, I'm coming.
  • Just a second.
  • Give me a minute.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Wait.

✅ Just a second.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Native speakers often soften "wait" with "just" or "one moment."

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• एक मिनट...
  • बीच में बोल रहा हूँ...
  • माफ़ कीजिए, लेकिन...
  • बीच में टोक रहा हूँ...

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Sorry to interrupt.
  • Excuse me.
  • If I may...
  • Can I jump in for a second?
  • May I add something?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Use these expressions to enter a conversation politely without sounding rude.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Sorry to interrupt, but I have a quick question.
  • Excuse me, may I add something?
  • Can I jump in for a second?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ I am cutting your talk.

✅ Sorry to interrupt.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Apologize briefly before interrupting.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• तो मैं कह रहा था...
  • जहाँ थे वहीं से...
  • हाँ, तो...
  • वैसे...

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Anyway...
  • As I was saying...
  • So, where were we?
  • Getting back to...
  • To continue...

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: These help you return to the original topic after an interruption.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Anyway, as I was saying...
  • So, where were we?
  • Getting back to the report...

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ As I was telling.

✅ As I was saying.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: "As I was saying..." is the classic way to resume.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• समझ गया।
  • ठीक है।
  • अच्छा।
  • समझ में आ गया।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Got it.
  • I understand.
  • That makes sense.
  • Okay, I see.
  • Understood.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Choose the expression based on formality. "Got it" is conversational; "Understood" is more formal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Got it. I'll do that.
  • Okay, I see.
  • That makes sense.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ I understood.

✅ I understand. / Got it.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Use "Got it." for everyday conversations.

docs.title: Pattern Family 21 — Asking Someone to Repeat
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• फिर से बोलो।
  • दोबारा कहना।
  • एक बार और बोलोगे?
  • क्या कहा?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Could you say that again?
  • Sorry, could you repeat that?
  • I didn't catch that.
  • Could you say that one more time?
  • Sorry?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Use polite forms in professional settings. "Sorry?" is common in casual conversations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Sorry, could you repeat that?
  • I didn't catch that.
  • Could you say that again?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Repeat again.

✅ Could you repeat that?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Ask to repeat that, not "again" after repeat.

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text: Most common: See Natural English Expressions above.

docs.title: Pattern Family 22 — Checking If You Heard Correctly
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• मैंने सही सुना?
  • मतलब...?
  • तुम कह रहे हो कि...?
  • क्या तुमने कहा...?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Did I hear that right?
  • So, you're saying...?
  • Did you say...?
  • Just to make sure...

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Use these to confirm important information before responding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Did I hear that right?
  • So, you're saying the meeting is tomorrow?
  • Just to make sure...

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ I heard correct?

✅ Did I hear that right?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Confirm before assuming.

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text: Most common: See Natural English Expressions above.

docs.title: Pattern Family 23 — Asking Someone to Speak More Slowly
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• थोड़ा धीरे बोलिए।
  • ज़रा धीरे बोलो।
  • बहुत तेज़ बोल रहे हो।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Could you speak a little more slowly?
  • Would you mind slowing down?
  • You're speaking a bit fast.
  • Could you slow down a little?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Be polite when asking someone to slow down.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Could you slow down a little?
  • You're speaking a bit fast.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Speak slow.

✅ Speak more slowly.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Prefer "slow down" in conversation.

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text: Most common: See Natural English Expressions above.

docs.title: Pattern Family 24 — Asking Someone to Speak Louder
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• ज़रा ज़ोर से बोलो।
  • आवाज़ नहीं आ रही।
  • थोड़ा ऊँचा बोलिए।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Could you speak up?
  • I can't hear you.
  • Could you speak a little louder?
  • Your voice is very soft.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: "Speak up" is the most natural everyday expression.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Could you speak up?
  • I can't hear you.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Speak loudly.

✅ Could you speak up?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: "Speak up" is the idiomatic choice.

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text: Most common: See Natural English Expressions above.

docs.title: Pattern Family 25 — Confirming Everything Is Clear
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• सब क्लियर?
  • समझ आया?
  • सब ठीक?
  • कोई सवाल?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Is everything clear?
  • Does that make sense?
  • Any questions?
  • Are we on the same page?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Common in meetings, teaching and explanations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Does that make sense?
  • Any questions before we continue?
  • Are we on the same page?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Everything clear?

✅ Is everything clear?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Use a complete question in formal situations.

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text: Most common: See Natural English Expressions above.

docs.title: Pattern Family 26 — Asking for a Moment
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• एक सेकंड।
  • बस एक मिनट।
  • थोड़ा समय दो।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Just a moment.
  • Give me a second.
  • One moment, please.
  • Bear with me.
  • Give me a minute.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Use these when you need a brief pause before continuing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Just a moment.
  • Give me a second.
  • One moment, please.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Wait.

✅ Just a moment.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Use 'just' to soften the request.

docs.title: Pattern Family 27 — Checking If Someone Is Still There
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• हेलो?
  • सुन रहे हो?
  • लाइन पर हो?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Are you still there?
  • Can you still hear me?
  • Hello?
  • Are you with me?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Useful during phone and video calls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Are you still there?
  • Can you still hear me?
  • Hello?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Are you there only?

✅ Are you still there?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Ask about presence, not 'only'.

docs.title: Pattern Family 28 — Asking for a Quick Favor
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• एक काम करोगे?
  • एक मदद चाहिए।
  • एक छोटा सा काम था।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Could you do me a favor?
  • Can I ask a quick favor?
  • Could you help me with something?
  • Would you mind helping me?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Common before making a small request.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Could you do me a favor?
  • Can I ask a quick favor?
  • Could you help me with something?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Do one work.

✅ Could you do me a favor?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: 'Favor' is the natural word.

docs.title: Pattern Family 29 — Checking If Someone Is Following
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• समझ आ रहा है?
  • मेरी बात समझ रहे हो?
  • फॉलो कर रहे हो?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Are you following?
  • Does that make sense?
  • Are you with me?
  • Following so far?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Often used while explaining something.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Are you following?
  • Does that make sense?
  • Are you with me?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Are you understanding?

✅ Are you following?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Prefer 'following' while explaining.

docs.title: Pattern Family 30 — Inviting Someone to Continue
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• आगे बताओ।
  • फिर?
  • उसके बाद?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Go on.
  • Please continue.
  • And then?
  • What happened next?
  • I'm listening.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Encourages the speaker to continue.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Go on.
  • Please continue.
  • And then?

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Tell further.

✅ Go on.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: 'Go on' is the natural prompt.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• हम्म...
  • सोचने दो...
  • एक मिनट सोचूँ...

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Let me think.
  • Hmm...
  • Give me a second to think.
  • That's a good question.
  • Let me see.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Useful when you need a moment before answering.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let me think.
  • Hmm...
  • Give me a second to think.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Wait, I am thinking.

✅ Let me think.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: "Let me think" is the standard phrase.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• अच्छा?
  • सच में?
  • फिर?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Really?
  • Is that so?
  • No way!
  • Tell me more.
  • What happened next?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Shows curiosity and keeps the conversation going.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Really?
  • Is that so?
  • No way!

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Tell further.

✅ Tell me more.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Ask naturally to encourage the speaker.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• अरे वाह!
  • सच में!
  • क्या बात है!

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Wow!
  • Really?
  • That's amazing!
  • No way!
  • You've got to be kidding!

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Different expressions fit different levels of surprise.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Wow!
  • Really?
  • That's amazing!

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ What a thing!

✅ Wow!

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Use short reactions.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• हाँ सही है।
  • बिल्कुल।
  • ठीक है।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• Exactly.
  • Absolutely.
  • I agree.
  • Sounds good.
  • You're right.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Common responses in everyday conversations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Exactly.
  • Absolutely.
  • I agree.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ I am agree.

✅ I agree.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Never use 'I am agree'.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• हूँ।
  • अच्छा।
  • समझ गया।
  • हम्म।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• I see.
  • Uh-huh.
  • Right.
  • Got it.
  • I understand.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: These listener responses keep the conversation flowing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• I see.
  • Uh-huh.
  • Right.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Yes only.

✅ I see.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Small acknowledgements sound natural.

docs.title: Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• ऐसा नहीं है।
  • मुझे नहीं लगता।
  • मैं सहमत नहीं हूँ।

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• I'm not so sure about that.
  • I don't think so.
  • I see it differently.
  • I'm afraid I disagree.
  • Not necessarily.

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Disagree without sounding confrontational.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• I'm not so sure about that.
  • I don't think so.
  • I see it differently.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ You are wrong.

✅ I'm not so sure about that.

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Disagree with the idea, not the person.

docs.title: Pattern Family 37 — Asking for Someone's Opinion
Hindi Pattern
docs.text:
• तुम्हारा क्या कहना है?
  • तुम्हें क्या लगता है?
  • क्या राय है?

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text:
• What do you think?
  • What's your opinion?
  • How do you see it?
  • What's your take?
  • Any thoughts?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text: Invite the other person to share their view.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• What do you think?
  • What's your opinion?
  • How do you see it?

docs.text: • High-Frequency Hindi Thoughts During First Conversations

docs.title: Hindi Thinking Pattern
docs.text:
When meeting someone for the first time, Hindi speakers often think:

  • नमस्ते बोल दूँ।
  • हेलो बोल देता हूँ।
  • बात शुरू करूँ?
  • कुछ तो बोलना चाहिए।
  • पहले विश कर लेता हूँ।
  • कैसे शुरुआत करूँ?
  • मैं ही बात शुरू करूँ?
  • शायद इन्हें भी बात करनी हो।
  • अभी बोलना ठीक रहेगा?
  • चुप रहना थोड़ा अजीब लग रहा है।

Core intention

You are not trying to introduce yourself yet.

You simply want to open the conversation politely.

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register When to use Hi! Casual Friends, neighbours, classmates Hello! Neutral Almost any situation Good morning. Neutral Morning meetings, office Good afternoon. Neutral Professional settings Good evening. Neutral Evening events Hi there! Casual Friendly informal interaction Excuse me... Neutral Before asking a question Mind if I join you? Polite Joining someone

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
Native English speakers rarely search for a "perfect opening sentence."

Most conversations begin with a simple greeting. The greeting is not meant to impress anyone—it simply signals that you're open to talking.

Hindi speakers sometimes delay speaking because they're trying to remember the "correct English." Native speakers generally value friendliness much more than perfection.

Hi, good morning!

docs.title: Common Thinking Traps
docs.text:
❌ Myself Vivek.

✅ Hi, I'm Vivek.

Why?

Native speakers introduce themselves using I'm..., not Myself...

❌ Good morning dear friend.

✅ Good morning!

Why?

English greetings are usually short and natural.

❌ Can I do friendship with you?

✅ Hi, I'm Vivek. Nice to meet you.

Why?

Friendships develop naturally. They are rarely announced.

docs.text: Expression Best used when Hi Everyday conversations Hello Safe in almost every situation Good morning Professional morning interactions Hi there Friendly informal tone Excuse me Getting someone's attention first

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text:
Don't think:

"Which English sentence should I remember?"

Think:

"I just need to acknowledge the other person."

A simple Hi is often enough.

  • Safest: Hello!

  • Key takeaway: Start the interaction simply. The conversation can grow naturally after the greeting.

  • अब क्या बोलूँ?

  • चुप्पी अजीब लग रही है।

  • कार्यक्रम अच्छा लग रहा है।
  • पहले माहौल हल्का करते हैं।
  • सीधे काम की बात करूँ या नहीं?

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
Small talk is rarely about the topic itself. A comment about the weather or the venue is simply an invitation to continue talking.

Native speakers usually choose topics that are visible to both people. This makes it easy for either person to continue—or politely end—the conversation.

  • आपका नाम क्या है?

  • किस कंपनी में हैं?

  • पढ़ाई कर रहे हैं या काम?

  • बातचीत आगे बढ़ाते हैं।

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
English conversations usually alternate between asking and sharing.

Instead of asking five questions in a row, native speakers often answer their own question after the other person responds.

Example:

A: Where are you from?

B: Pune.

A: Nice! I'm from Delhi.

That keeps the conversation balanced.

Situation

You meet someone during a workshop.

Hindi Thought

आप क्या करते हैं?

Your Natural English

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
• Most useful: What do you do?
  • Safest: Where are you from?
  • Avoid: "What is your good name?" and literal Hindi word order.
  • Key takeaway: Balance curiosity with sharing about yourself.

docs.title: Hindi Thinking Pattern
docs.text:
When two people don't know each other, Hindi speakers often think:

  • इन दोनों का परिचय करा देता हूँ।
  • इन्हें मिलवाना चाहिए।
  • ये भी एक-दूसरे के काम आ सकते हैं।
  • शायद इनकी अच्छी बनेगी।
  • दोनों एक ही क्षेत्र में हैं।
  • पहले इनका परिचय करा दूँ।
  • मिल लीजिए एक-दूसरे से।
  • आप दोनों पहले नहीं मिले?

Core intention

Help two people become comfortable by giving enough context for them to start talking.

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register When to use Have you two met? Casual Friends, family I'd like you to meet Rahul. Neutral Most situations This is Neha from our design team. Neutral Office Let me introduce you to... Formal Meetings, events You both work in AI, don't you? Casual Creating connection I think you'll get along. Casual Friends, networking

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
Native speakers usually provide context, not just names.

Instead of saying only:

This is Rahul.

they often add one useful detail:

This is Rahul. We worked together at Amazon.

That gives both people an easy place to continue the conversation.

docs.text:
Hindi Thought

इन दोनों का परिचय करा देता हूँ।

A: Sarah, I'd like you to meet Rahul.

B: Nice to meet you.

C: Nice to meet you too.

docs.title: Conference
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

दोनों एक ही क्षेत्र में हैं।

A: You both work in cloud engineering. I thought you should meet.

B: Great to meet you.

C: Likewise.

docs.title: Family Gathering
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

पहले मिलवा देता हूँ।

A: Have you two met before?

B: I don't think so.

A: This is my cousin, Amit.

docs.title: Friends
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

शायद इनकी अच्छी बनेगी।

A: I think you two have a lot in common.

B: Really?

C: Let's find out.

docs.title: Customer Visit
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

इनसे मिलिए।

A: Let me introduce you to our project manager.

B: Pleasure to meet you.

C: Likewise.

docs.title: Common Thinking Traps
docs.text:
❌ Meet with my friend.

✅ I'd like you to meet my friend.

Why? "Meet with" means to have a meeting. Here you're introducing people.

❌ He is my childhood friend only.

✅ He's a childhood friend of mine.

Why? Avoid adding "only" for emphasis.

❌ Both are same field.

✅ You both work in the same field.

Why? Complete the sentence naturally.

docs.title: Similar Expressions
docs.text: Expression Best used when This is... Quick introductions I'd like you to meet... Polite introductions Let me introduce you to... Formal settings Have you two met? Checking before introducing

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Don't just exchange names. Give one small piece of context that helps the conversation continue.

docs.title: Thinking Pattern 005 — Keeping the Conversation Alive
Hindi Thinking Pattern
docs.text:
Once the conversation is flowing, Hindi speakers often think:

  • अब आगे क्या बोलूँ?
  • बातचीत रुकनी नहीं चाहिए।
  • थोड़ा और पूछ लेता हूँ।
  • इनके बारे में और जानूँ।
  • अच्छा, फिर क्या हुआ?
  • सच में?
  • और बताइए।
  • अच्छा लग रहा है, बात जारी रखते हैं.
  • अब विषय कैसे बदलूँ?
  • बातचीत चलती रहनी चाहिए।

Core intention

Keep the other person engaged without making the conversation feel like an interview.

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register When to use Really? Casual Showing surprise or interest That sounds interesting. Neutral Encouraging the speaker Tell me more. Neutral Inviting more details How did that happen? Neutral Following up What was that like? Neutral Asking about experiences How about you? Casual Returning the conversation

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
Good conversations move back and forth. Native speakers rarely ask a long list of unrelated questions. They react first, then ask a follow-up.

Instead of:

Where are you from? What do you do? Are you married?

they naturally build on the previous answer.

docs.title: Office
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

और बताइए।

A: I joined the team last month.

B: That's great. How are you finding it so far?

docs.title: Conference
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

फिर क्या हुआ?

A: We recently launched a new product.

B: Nice! How did it go?

docs.title: Coffee Break
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

सच में?

A: I just got back from Japan.

B: Really? What was your favourite part?

docs.title: Family Gathering
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

बातचीत जारी रखते हैं।

A: We moved to Bengaluru this year.

B: Oh, how are you liking it?

docs.title: Messaging
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

थोड़ा और पूछता हूँ।

A: I finally finished the marathon.

B: That's impressive! How long did it take?

docs.title: Common Thinking Traps
docs.text:
❌ And then? And then? And then?

✅ What happened after that?

Why? Repeat questions can sound unnatural.

❌ Tell everything.

✅ Tell me more.

Why? "Tell me more" is a polite invitation.

❌ What else?

✅ Anything else interesting happen?

Why? Give the speaker a natural opening.

docs.title: Similar Expressions
docs.text: Expression Best used when Really? Showing genuine interest Tell me more. Inviting details What was that like? Asking about experiences How about you? Bringing balance back to the conversation

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Don't prepare your next question while the other person is speaking. Listen first, then react to what they actually said.

docs.text:

  • Safest: That sounds interesting.

docs.title: Hindi Thinking Pattern
docs.text:
As the conversation becomes comfortable, Hindi speakers often think:

  • अरे, ये तो मेरी तरह हैं।
  • हमारी तो काफी बातें मिलती हैं।
  • मुझे भी यही पसंद है।
  • हम दोनों एक ही शहर के हैं।
  • हमारी फील्ड भी एक जैसी है।
  • इनसे फिर बात करनी चाहिए।
  • अच्छी बातचीत हो रही है।
  • इनसे जुड़ाव महसूस हो रहा है.
  • हम दोनों का अनुभव मिलता-जुलता है।
  • ये तो मज़ेदार संयोग है।

Core intention

Move beyond exchanging information and create a genuine personal connection.

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register When to use Me too! Casual Shared interests Same here. Casual Similar opinions or experiences We have that in common. Neutral Shared background I know exactly what you mean. Neutral Shared experience I've always wanted to try that. Neutral Showing interest That's something we both enjoy. Professional Networking

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
People usually connect over similarities, not impressive stories. Even a small shared experience can make a conversation warmer.

Rather than changing the subject, acknowledge the connection before moving on.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

हम दोनों Java में हैं।

A: I work mostly with Java.

B: Me too! I've been working with Java for years.

docs.title: Travel
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

मैं भी वहाँ गया हूँ।

A: I visited Jaipur last month.

B: Same here. I loved the old city.

docs.title: Office
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

हम दोनों को कॉफी पसंद है।

A: I can't start my day without coffee.

B: Me neither.

docs.title: Friends
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

मुझे भी क्रिकेट पसंद है।

A: I watch almost every cricket match.

B: Me too!

docs.title: Conference
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

हम दोनों पहली बार आए हैं।

A: This is my first conference.

B: Mine too.

docs.title: Common Thinking Traps
docs.text:
❌ We both are same.

✅ We're quite similar.

Why? Native speakers describe the similarity, not "same" as a noun.

❌ Same pinch!

✅ Me too! / Same here.

Why? "Same pinch" is not common in everyday native English.

❌ Our thinking matches.

✅ We think alike.

Why? This is the natural idiomatic expression.

docs.title: Similar Expressions
docs.text: Expression Best used when Me too! Shared actions or likes Same here. Shared opinions We have that in common. Shared background I know exactly what you mean. Shared experiences

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: Connection grows when you notice similarities. Respond to what you share before introducing a new topic.

docs.title: Mini Practice
docs.text:
Situation

Someone says, "I love hiking on weekends."

Hindi Thought

मुझे भी ट्रेकिंग पसंद है।

Your Natural English

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
• Most useful: Me too!
  • Safest: We have that in common.
  • Avoid: Literal expressions like "Same pinch."
  • Key takeaway: Shared experiences build rapport naturally.

docs.title: Thinking Pattern 007 — Ending the Conversation Politely
Hindi Thinking Pattern
docs.text:
As a conversation comes to a natural end, Hindi speakers often think:

  • अब चलता हूँ।
  • अब निकलना चाहिए।
  • अच्छा लगा आपसे मिलकर।
  • फिर मिलते हैं।
  • अब मुझे जाना होगा।
  • देर हो रही है।
  • आपको रोकना नहीं चाहता।
  • अब आपकी छुट्टी।
  • उम्मीद है फिर मुलाकात होगी।
  • बातचीत अच्छी लगी।

Core intention

End the conversation in a warm, natural way without sounding abrupt or making the other person feel dismissed.

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register When to use It was nice talking to you. Neutral Almost any conversation It was great meeting you. Neutral First meetings I'd better get going. Casual Leaving naturally I'll let you get back to it. Professional When someone is busy Enjoy the rest of your day. Neutral Friendly closing Have a safe trip. Neutral Travel See you around. Casual Friends, colleagues Take care. Neutral Everyday conversations

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
Native speakers usually give a small reason before leaving.

Instead of suddenly saying "Bye", they often soften the ending.

Examples:

  • I'd better get going.
  • I should let you get back to work.
  • I won't keep you any longer.

This makes the conversation feel complete instead of interrupted.

docs.title: Office
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

अब आपको काम करने देता हूँ।

A: I'll let you get back to work.

B: Thanks. It was nice talking to you.

docs.title: Conference
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

अच्छा लगा आपसे मिलकर।

A: It was great meeting you.

B: Likewise. Enjoy the conference.

docs.title: Coffee Shop
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

अब चलता हूँ।

A: I'd better get going.

B: Sure. Take care.

docs.title: Airport
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

आपकी फ्लाइट अच्छी रहे।

A: Have a safe trip.

B: Thanks! You too.

docs.title: Family Function
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

फिर मिलते हैं।

A: It was lovely meeting you.

B: Hope to see you again soon.

docs.title: Common Thinking Traps
docs.text:
❌ Bye only.

✅ Bye! Take care.

Why?

Adding a short closing phrase sounds warmer and more natural.

❌ We will meet.

✅ See you around.

Why?

English usually uses a conversational farewell rather than a literal future statement.

❌ I am going.

✅ I'd better get going.

Why?

Native speakers often soften the departure instead of announcing it directly.

docs.title: Similar Expressions
docs.text: Expression Best used when It was nice talking to you. General conversations It was great meeting you. First meetings I'd better get going. Casual departures I'll let you get back to work. Professional settings Take care. Universal farewell

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text:
Don't end a conversation suddenly.

Give a short closing remark, wish the other person well, and then leave.

docs.title: Mini Practice
docs.text:
Situation

You've been chatting with a colleague for ten minutes, but both of you need to return to work.

Hindi Thought

अब आपको काम करने देता हूँ।

Your Natural English

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
• Most useful: It was nice talking to you.
  • Safest: Take care.
  • Avoid: Literal endings like "We will meet."
  • Key takeaway: A polite ending leaves a positive final impression.

docs.title: Hindi Thinking Pattern
docs.text:
When a conversation has gone well, Hindi speakers often think:

  • इनसे फिर बात करनी चाहिए।
  • नंबर ले लेता हूँ।
  • संपर्क में रहेंगे।
  • LinkedIn पर जुड़ जाते हैं।
  • कभी मिलते हैं।
  • आपका नंबर मिल सकता है?
  • संपर्क बना रहता है।
  • आगे भी बात करेंगे।
  • फिर मिलते हैं।
  • अच्छा लगा, जुड़े रहते हैं।

Core intention

The conversation is ending, but you would like the relationship to continue in the future.

docs.title: Natural English Expressions
docs.text: Expression Register When to use Let's keep in touch. Neutral Friends and colleagues Here's my number. Casual After a good conversation Are you on LinkedIn? Professional Networking events I'd love to stay in touch. Neutral Professional and social Feel free to reach out. Professional Business conversations Let's catch up sometime. Casual Existing acquaintances It would be great to connect. Professional Conferences

docs.title: Nuance
docs.text:
Native speakers usually make the next step specific.

Instead of saying only "We'll stay in touch," they often suggest how:

  • Connect on LinkedIn
  • Exchange numbers
  • Share an email
  • Plan to catch up

A concrete action makes the invitation feel genuine.

docs.title: Conference
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

LinkedIn पर जुड़ जाते हैं।

A: Are you on LinkedIn?

B: Yes, let me send you a connection request.

docs.title: Office Meetup
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

संपर्क में रहेंगे।

A: Let's keep in touch.

B: Absolutely.

docs.title: Coffee Chat
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

नंबर ले लेता हूँ।

A: Here's my number.

B: Thanks. I'll save it.

docs.title: Client Meeting
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

ज़रूरत हो तो संपर्क कीजिए।

A: Feel free to reach out if you need anything.

B: I appreciate that.

docs.title: Networking Event
docs.text:
Hindi Thought

फिर कभी मिलते हैं।

A: Let's catch up sometime.

B: I'd like that.

docs.title: Common Thinking Traps
docs.text:
❌ We will always be in contact.

✅ Let's keep in touch.

Why?

English prefers simple, natural expressions.

❌ Give me your contact.

✅ Could I have your number?

Why?

A polite request sounds much more natural.

❌ Message me compulsory.

✅ Drop me a message sometime.

Why?

Avoid direct commands when making friendly invitations.

docs.title: Similar Expressions
docs.text: Expression Best used when Let's keep in touch. General situations Are you on LinkedIn? Professional networking Feel free to reach out. Clients and colleagues Let's catch up sometime. Friends and acquaintances

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text: If you genuinely want to stay connected, suggest one simple next step instead of making a vague promise.

docs.title: Mini Practice
docs.text:
Situation

Hindi Thought

LinkedIn पर जुड़ जाते हैं।

docs.title: Quick Recap
docs.text:
• Most useful: Let's keep in touch.
  • Safest: Are you on LinkedIn?
  • Avoid: Literal translations like "Give me your contact."
  • Key takeaway: End the conversation with a clear and natural way to continue the relationship.

docs.title: Thinking Pattern 009 — High-Frequency Hindi Thoughts During First Conversations
Why this Pattern Exists
docs.text:
This chapter already covers the major thinking patterns of introductions and small talk.

This supplementary pattern captures dozens of high-frequency Hindi thoughts that naturally occur during first meetings but don't justify separate thinking patterns.

Use it as a quick-reference companion.

docs.title: Starting the Interaction
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English नमस्ते बोल दूँ। I'll say hi. हेलो बोल देता हूँ। Hi! एक्सक्यूज़ मी। Excuse me. आपको डिस्टर्ब तो नहीं कर रहा? Am I catching you at a bad time? दो मिनट मिलेंगे? Do you have a minute? क्या अभी बात कर सकते हैं? Is now a good time?

docs.title: Breaking the Ice
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English बहुत भीड़ है। It's quite busy today. काफी ट्रैफिक था। Traffic was terrible today. यहाँ पहली बार आए हैं? Is this your first time here? रास्ता आसानी से मिल गया? Did you find the place easily? लाइन काफी लंबी है। That's quite a long line. मौसम अच्छा है। Nice weather today.

docs.title: Getting to Know Someone
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English आपका नाम क्या है? What's your name? आप कहाँ से हैं? Where are you from? क्या करते हैं? What do you do? किस कंपनी में हैं? Which company do you work for? यहीं रहते हैं? Do you live nearby? यहाँ कैसे आना हुआ? What brings you here?

docs.title: Keeping the Conversation Going
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English अच्छा? Oh, really? फिर? And then? / What happened next? सच में? Really? उसके बाद? What happened after that? वाह! That's great! कमाल है। That's amazing! और बताइए। Tell me more.

docs.title: Building a Connection
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English मुझे भी। Me too. मेरे साथ भी ऐसा हुआ। The same thing happened to me. बिल्कुल। Absolutely. मेरी भी यही राय है। I feel the same way. मुझे भी पसंद है। I like it too. हम दोनों एक ही शहर के हैं। We're from the same city.

docs.title: Ending the Conversation
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English अब चलता हूँ। I'd better get going. अच्छा लगा आपसे मिलकर। It was great meeting you. फिर मिलते हैं। See you around. ध्यान रखिए। Take care. घर पहुँचकर बताइए। Let me know when you get home.

docs.title: Staying Connected
docs.text: Hindi Thought Natural English संपर्क में रहेंगे। Let's keep in touch. नंबर सेव कर लीजिए। Save my number. मुझे मैसेज कर देना। Drop me a message. LinkedIn पर जुड़ते हैं। Let's connect on LinkedIn. कभी कॉफी पर मिलते हैं। Let's grab a coffee sometime.

docs.title: Common Indian English vs Natural English
docs.text: Common Indian English Natural English What is your good name? What's your name? I belong to Delhi. I'm from Delhi. I am doing a job. I work as... / I have a job. Can we do friendship? Let's keep in touch. Where do you do job? Where do you work?

docs.title: Memory Tip
docs.text:
Don't memorize every sentence.

Recognize the Hindi thought, identify the communication goal, then choose the English expression that feels most natural for the situation.
